title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding and agent tool being used as an active component in offensive cyber operations. Cursor Agent, running Claude Sonnet, was used by ransomware operators to conduct hands-on exploitation against target organizations. The tool was not compromised or modified, it was simply directed toward malicious tasks in the same way a legitimate user might direct it toward development work. The failure is not one of model safety controls catching an edge case, it is a case of a capable agentic tool being operated by actors with harmful intent within its normal functional range.

The deployment gap here is the absence of use-case enforcement at the point of operation. Agentic AI tools that can browse, execute code, and interact with external systems create a surface that is difficult to distinguish from legitimate use during any single session. Catching this would have required either behavioral monitoring across sessions, anomaly detection on the types of tasks being submitted, or external threat intelligence connecting tool activity to known attack infrastructure. None of those controls are standard features of such tools.

What is not established is whether Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, had any knowledge of this use, or whether the observed activity constitutes a legal finding against any named individual or group. The reporting comes from security researchers, not from law enforcement or judicial proceedings.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi virtual environments. Between April and May 2026, the group used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation against ten organizations. The ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption and includes an ESXi mode that terminates virtual machines to unlock files for encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. A custom tool called esxi_finder.py scans networks to locate ESXi hosts and vCenter servers by checking ports 443 and 902.

Researchers identified a second Aurora cluster operating separately, targeting eight organizations across multiple countries including Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This second group used different tactics including SQL Server exploitation and DCSync attacks for data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation provided multiple indicators of compromise, including IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes associated with both Aurora clusters to help organizations identify and defend against these threats.
